entities.name: Book of Rites
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Book of Rites (, Lǐjì) is a collection of ancient Chinese texts that date back to the Zhou Dynasty (1046–256 BCE). These texts were compiled and interpreted during the Warring States Period (475–221 BCE) and the Early Han Dynasty (206 BCE–220 CE), providing valuable insights into the social forms, administrative structures, and ceremonial rites of the Zhou Dynasty.

    The Book of Rites was compiled by various scholars and officials during the Han Dynasty, who drew upon earlier texts and oral traditions to create a comprehensive guide to the rituals and practices of the Zhou Dynasty. The text is divided into 39 chapters, each covering a specific aspect of Zhou ritual and practice.

    The Book of Rites had a profound impact on Chinese culture and society, shaping the development of Confucianism and influencing the way in which the Chinese people understood their place in the world. Its influence can still be seen in modern-day China, where the text remains an important source of cultural and historical knowledge.

    Despite its importance, the Book of Rites was largely forgotten during the Tang Dynasty (618–907 CE), but was rediscovered during the Song Dynasty (960–1279 CE), when it became a central text of Confucian studies.

    The Book of Rites is considered one of the most important sources of information on the Zhou Dynasty, providing a unique window into the culture and society of ancient China.
